description: I'm Taimour, a software engineer in Islamabad. I build AI agents and workflow automation in Python, FastAPI and React, and took part in Space Apps 2025. We are taking on Flame in Freefall: an LLM-powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks and compares NASA's microgravity combustion experiments. I will cover the backend and LLM pipeline. Looking for teammates in frontend, data visualization, data analysis and design. We work fully online and the deadline is close, so join if you can start now.
summary:
NASA set almost a metre of cotton and fiberglass fabric on fire on a cargo ship, after it left the Space Station. It is one of 263 material fire tests in NASA's data, and every one of them burned in the same kind of air: Space Station air, normal pressure, 14 to 22% oxygen.

The places people want to live next are a bit different. NASA plans Moon and Mars habitats at 34% oxygen and 0.56 atm, and no material fire in the data we used comes near it.

So we built a page that asks one question: would this burn here? You pick a material and a place, or ask about something you own ("would my running shoe burn in a Moon rover?"). The answer is one of two: "NASA tested this", or "We don't know. No matching test." It sounds like a small answer. Turns out it is the finding.

The AI only works out what your object is made of. The verdict, the numbers and the charts come from NASA's own tables.
details:
What it does

The page asks "would this burn here?" for a material and a place: Earth, the Space Station, spacewalk prep, a Moon base, a pressurized rover or a Mars base. It answers in one of two ways. "NASA tested this" means real fires with that material burned in air like that place's. "We don't know. No matching test." means NASA tested the material, but only in different air. Not tested here does not mean safe. Tested does not mean safe either, which is why every verdict links to the experiments behind it.

The first screen holds the whole argument in one picture. Each blue dot on the oxygen strip is a real NASA fire, and the diamond is the air of the place you chose. When no dot sits near the diamond, nobody in the data has tested that air. Below it, five tabs look closer:

  • The gap: every material fire by oxygen and cabin pressure. They sit at about 1 atm, and the places people plan to live sit somewhere else.
  • Experiments: the 24 investigations, ranked for the place you chose and sorted into prevent, detect and suppress. Each summary line shows the part of the NASA record it comes from.
  • A real fire: the four heat sensors of Saffire-I, replayed. Two warm first, the other two about two minutes later. That is the flame moving.
  • Back on Earth: where space fire safety came home (water-mist extinguishers, smoke detectors, firefighters' air tanks, protective clothing).
  • The data: the tests for each material, as a chart, a table and a CSV file.

At the bottom, a question box takes everyday questions, such as "Will an NVIDIA H100 GPU burn on Mars?".

How it works

We started in two notebooks. The first explores NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics combustion records: 24 investigations, with their test tables, papers and raw files. The second cleans those tables into one table of 263 material tests. The air of each place comes from NASA technical reports.

The AI does one task, and on purpose a small one: it names the materials of an object ("a plastic shroud, a circuit board, a metal heatsink"). A fixed table in our code then picks the nearest material NASA tested. The AI never decides the verdict. If nothing in the data is similar (a metal spoon, water), the page says so. Fourteen everyday questions check the AI after each change.

The site is Vue 3 and Vite, with SVG and D3 charts, and it works without a network connection. The question service is FastAPI and LangGraph with a DeepSeek model.

Why it matters

We know a great deal about fire in one kind of air, and almost nothing about the air we are about to live in. We wanted that gap to be the first thing you see, and we wanted the page to say "we don't know" when that is the honest answer.

Limits

NASA's tables do not record the pressure of the material tests, so we use cabin pressure (about 1 atm), and the page shows this. "No matching test" applies only to the data we used. The Moon, rover and Mars atmospheres are proposals; real missions can be different. The experiment summaries were written by AI from NASA's records. Each line shows the part of the record it comes from, and our code removed every line without a real source. Read them before you quote them.
